merchant-manual.label: Unit-rate manual: divide, then scale
merchant-manual.description: The worked example and general reasoning serve a second account rather than requiring a new memorized answer.

reading.text: Three equal cloth lengths cost 18 units: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 units per length; five lengths cost 5 × 6 = 30. The general calculation keeps the quantities and their units together: total amount ÷ number of equal units gives an amount per unit; multiply that rate by the new number of units. This is the worked merchant example joined to the earlier general algebraic method, not a new memorized answer.
reading.attribution: Authored merchant-arithmetic worksheet, not a quotation from Fibonacci. Reuse in later calculations is a pedagogical connection, not a claim that this particular manual was transmitted.

circulating-arithmetic.label: Circulating arithmetic book
circulating-arithmetic.description: Practical arithmetic becomes portable without making every future reader agree with every rule.

illustration-method.label: Courtyard plate: E alignment + S mismatch recorded
illustration-method.description: Keep the painting with its viewing conditions: eye E, height 2; panel 2 ahead; post 4 ahead; doorway 8 ahead. The post edge and far jamb coincide at x=0 from E. With only the eye shifted 2 right to S, their real crossings become x=1 and x=1½, while the painted marks stay together. A later reader can distinguish the constructed view from this comparison and from depths supplied by the plan. This is a reusable way to document an explanatory image, not a rule that all art must use linear perspective.

algebra-method.label: Halve, square, add, root, subtract: second side y=2
algebra-method.description: For a positive-length problem u²+bu=c with b and c positive, halve b; add the square (b/2)² to both equal areas; take the positive square root; subtract b/2. In modern notation: u=√(c+(b/2)²)−b/2. The repaired equality rules explain why the same area is added to both sides, and the filled first diagram explains why that area completes a square. First plot: √(40+9)−3=4, checked by 16+24=40. Second supplied plot: half of 8 is 4; 20+16=36; the positive outer side is √36=6; then y=6−4=2; check 2²+8×2=4+16=20. This reusable algebra also keeps quantities and units attached to an unknown; applying the same valid operation to both sides, including division by the same nonzero number, preserves an equality. The geometric argument here addresses positive lengths, not every signed or complex root.

reading.text: This table represents accurately recorded planetary positions made before the telescope. A later instrument does not make careful earlier observations valueless. A model must answer positional discrepancies as well as familiar periodic returns.

counterexample.label: One uncovered lamp breaks the “every darkening” claim
counterexample.description: The single case defeats this universal premise, not all accounts of eclipses.

reading.text: The lamp darkens without being covered. Thus it contradicts the claim that every darkening is caused by a cover. The reusable argument is that one genuine contrary case defeats an unrestricted universal statement; it need not defeat a narrower claim.
reading.attribution: Authored teaching reconstruction; not a historical quotation.

compound-rule.label: (A OR B) AND NOT C
compound-rule.description: Allow (A OR B) AND NOT C, where C means a blocking condition.

reading.text: Permit entry if A or B holds, including both, and C does not hold. The parentheses in (A OR B) AND NOT C determine which condition blocks the permission. Formal consistency does not establish that the entry policy is just.
reading.attribution: Authored binary-logic case; modern notation, not Boole’s original wording.
